title: Long context versus retrieval: scale boundaries

opening.headline: When deciding to transition from a structure that inserts documents en masse to a search-based structure, judgment is made based on scale and update frequency.
body: Initially, simply feeding all 100 documents directly into the prompt works well. However, as the number of documents grows and changes weekly, costs, delays, and accuracy begin to fluctuate. Without a clear criterion for when to switch to a search-based approach, one may either prematurely migrate, wasting setup costs, or delay the migration too long, resulting in reduced quality.

This course compares how context-aware and search-based approaches operate and what they gain and lose. It structures the discussion along two axes—document volume and update frequency—and then illustrates these concepts with examples of selections at scales of 100, 10,000, and 100,000 documents.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This explains how context-based and search-based approaches are appropriate according to scale.
Appropriate structures can be distinguished based on document volume and refresh intervals.

screens.title: Documents are increasing—when should we change the structure?
screens.lead: Consider the following scenario: how can you determine when it's necessary to change the structure?

visual.alt: A concept chart showing that as the number of documents increases, the cost per call for the bulk-insert approach rises while the cost for the search approach increases gradually, with the two lines intersecting.
labels: Search method (enter only a few upper pieces)

paragraphs: A team developed an internal document Q&A service. Initially, they inserted all 100 documents directly into the prompt, and it worked well. The structure was simple, and the model could view relationships between documents all at once.

As time passed, the documentation grew significantly and began to be updated weekly. With each call, the input cost increased, response times slowed down, and at some point, the accuracy of the responses started to degrade. It now seems necessary to transition to a search-based approach, but there is no clear benchmark. Moving early would result in unnecessary setup and operational costs, while delaying the transition would require accepting a decline in quality.

This course covers methods for identifying transition points based on two criteria: scale and update cycle. First, it explains the operational mechanisms of both structures, then outlines the signals that indicate when to switch between them.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will the transition point be defined by a single number such as "a few documents," or will it vary based on cost, delay, and update frequency? We'll look at a table answering this question during the lecture.

screens.outro: First, let's get a rough estimate of my current document volume.

screens.title: Think about whether the current document volume is being included in the context.
screens.lead: When a question is selected, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Since you don't need to enter or submit an answer, take a moment to think first and recall your own notes.

items.prompt: Is the current document volume sufficient to be fully included in the context?
items.answer: Multiply the number of pages by the number of tokens per page to estimate the total number of tokens. Gemini states that 1 million tokens correspond to an English novel of about eight volumes or five ten thousand lines of code. By comparing this scale with the total size of my document, you can get a general sense of whether it can be fully included. The exact value must be verified by manually counting the tokens.

items.prompt: How frequently is the document updated?
items.answer: The update frequency is the second criterion for determining the structure. The inline insertion method simply involves attaching the latest version with each request, making updates straightforward. The search-based method, however, requires re-partitioning, embedding, and indexing every time the document changes, thus necessitating an update pipeline.

items.prompt: Has the current architecture ever experienced fluctuations in cost or accuracy?
items.answer: Three signals indicate it's time to reconsider the structure: cost escalation, accuracy degradation, and feature overflow. If any of these are present, you should reassess scale and update frequency and reevaluate whether a transition is warranted. In this course's example walkthrough, each of these signals is revisited.

screens.outro: First, let's examine the approach of inserting the entire long context.

screens.title: Long context method: Insert as a whole
screens.lead: Compare selecting the two state buttons alternately to gain and lose a long context mode.

states.label: What you get
states.body: Gemini documents explain that with a large window of over 1M tokens, it is possible to perform long-text summarization, question-answering, and agent tasks by presenting all necessary information upfront for processing. Previously, due to small windows, question-answering relied on search-based methods; now, more direct approaches are feasible. Its simple structure allows the model to view relationships between documents at once, and it can be used without any code changes. When the entire document is presented at once, it becomes easier to answer questions that connect information scattered across multiple documents—something search-based methods might miss. Additionally, there's no need to build and maintain separate systems for segmentation, indexing, or search quality, enabling faster initial setup. Caching can significantly reduce costs and latency for repeated document inputs.

states.label: Losing something
states.body: Each call incurs additional input token costs. When only one piece of information is found in the document, accuracy is high; however, when multiple pieces of information are present, accuracy may not be consistent, and repeating the query to achieve high accuracy incurs input costs each time. There is also a phenomenon where accuracy and recall degrade as the number of tokens increases, and longer inputs result in slower responses. It is generally advised to place the question near the end of a long context. Finally, when a document exceeds the window size, the approach becomes impossible. In summary, the long-context approach is most appropriate when the document fits within the window and when the number of calls is low or when repeated queries can be mitigated through caching.

screens.outro: Now we will look at a search method that maintains consistent input even as the document volume increases.

screens.title: Search method: Retrieve only the required pieces
screens.lead: The following flashcard outlines the six sequential steps involved in processing documents through a search approach. When a card is selected, it flips over, and selecting the right arrow advances to the next card.

visual.alt: The flow involves collecting, splitting, embedding, and indexing documents for storage, and then proceeding to retrieval and generation when a query arrives.

cards.back: This is the step of gathering data from various sources such as local files, cloud storage, and document tools. It is the first step in the process described by the RAG Engine documentation, where the collected documents become the raw material for all subsequent steps. The scope of collection directly corresponds to the scope of knowledge that can be retrieved through search.

This is a transformation step that divides documents into chunks suitable for indexing. If chunks are too large, irrelevant content may be included; if too small, context may be broken. The chunking method is a new failure point that directly impacts search quality.

This step converts words or word fragments into numerical representations that carry meaning. Similar or related text is assigned similar numerical representations and placed close to each other in space. As a result, it is possible to find results with similar meanings even if the keywords differ.

This is the step of organizing and storing chunks and embeddings in a structure optimized for search. A document is analogous to a detailed table of contents of a large reference book. At OpenAI, a vector store performs this indexing role, and when files are added, they are automatically split, embedded, and indexed. Storage costs are charged based on the size of the stored chunks.

When a user question arrives, the step involves searching the index for relevant fragments related to the question. Searching with natural language queries returns relevant fragments along with similarity scores and original file information. You can also filter out fragments with low relevance using ranking adjustment options. A key advantage here is that the input consistently appears in the top few fragments for each request.

This step involves attaching the retrieved fragments back to the original question and passing them to the model to generate a well-reasoned answer. Since the model only references the content provided in the request, any content missed by the search will not be reflected in the answer. Therefore, segmentation, indexing, and search quality directly determine the quality of the final answer.

screens.outro: Now that I understand the behavior of both structures, I will compile a table to determine which structure is appropriate based on scale and update frequency.

screens.lead: The following table establishes an appropriate structure based on the document volume and update frequency. Read each of the four scenarios and verify where the transition point occurs.

data.notes: A transition point is not fixed to a single number. Instead, it is determined jointly by context window size, cost per query invocation, allowable delay, and indexing maintenance cost, with update frequency setting the indexing overhead. Therefore, in addition to document count, all three of these factors must be considered together. For example, if a document is queried at least thousands of times per day, the cumulative cost per query may make query-based retrieval more favorable. Conversely, even with a large number of documents, if there are few actual queries, the operational cost of maintaining an index may exceed the benefits. The four rows in the table represent starting points, and the actual selection is determined by substituting these three values.

screens.outro: Let's apply the judgment of the table to three cases of different scales.

screens.title: 100 items · 10,000 items · 1 million items of selective explanations
screens.lead: The instructor walks through the process of selecting a structure based on document scale. Select an arrow to proceed step by step and follow the rationale provided.

steps.title: Assumption: One document contains approximately 2,000 tokens
steps.body: To illustrate case sizes, we assume each document contains on average approximately 2,000 tokens. This value is illustrative and must be verified by actually counting tokens. Under this assumption, 100 documents amount to approximately 200,000 tokens, 10,000 documents amount to approximately 20 million tokens, and 1 million documents amount to approximately 2 billion tokens.

steps.title: 100 items: Insert all at once and cache
steps.body: Fits comfortably within a 1M token context window using approximately 200,000 tokens. We opt for the simplest structure—direct insertion—while caching previous inputs to reduce input costs and latency when the same query is repeated. Questions are placed at the end of the context. If the document frequently changes, the latest version is appended with each request.

steps.title: 10,000 records: exceeds window limit, thus requiring basic search method
steps.body: Approximately 2 million tokens is 20 times more than 1 million tokens. Since it's impossible to ingest all content at once, a search-based approach becomes the default. At this scale, we must design a chunking strategy, index update frequency, and search quality evaluation. If documents are frequently updated, we also establish a mechanism to reindex only the changed documents.

steps.title: 1 million records: Indexing operations in addition to searching
steps.body: When reaching approximately 2 billion tokens, you must consider index size and storage costs, update pipelines, and large-scale vector search infrastructure. Google Cloud provides an RAG infrastructure architecture that stores vector embeddings alongside operational data in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL or Cloud SQL. At this scale, schema selection becomes directly tied to operational design.

steps.title: Transition signals common to all three sizes
steps.body: When both scale and update frequency are high, the cost of rebuilding the index dominates the structure. Signals indicating that the structure needs to be changed are three: a sharp increase in cost per call, a drop in accuracy, or documents exceeding the window size. When such signals are detected, the scale and update frequency are re-evaluated and moved to the corresponding row in the table.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: Scale and update frequency define the structure.
screens.lead: This lesson's key points are summarized. Please review your answers to the questions posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: These two approaches are not about superiority but about differing conditions. If the document is short and stable, a simple, context-lengthening approach is sufficient. If the document exceeds a window size or incurs high input costs per invocation, a search-based approach is more appropriate. The mere appearance of a large window does not eliminate the need for search, and search is not always more accurate. If context is broken by chunking, search may fail.

The context-length approach incurs input costs on each call, may degrade accuracy and recall as token count increases, and cannot be used beyond a given context window. The retrieval approach maintains constant input cost even as document volume grows, but introduces new stages—collection, splitting, embedding, indexing, and retrieval—along with the operational overhead associated with them.

Going back to the initial question, the transition point is not a single number but a set of parameters including window size, cost per call, allowable latency, and update frequency. Cost spikes, accuracy degradation, and window overflow serve as transition signals; upon observing such signals, the document volume and update frequency should be re-evaluated and the overall structure adjusted accordingly.

Finally, after restructuring, compare the quality of answers using the same set of questions. The purpose of restructuring is not merely to reduce costs, but also to aim for both accuracy and latency. You can verify whether the rearchitecture was appropriate by comparing performance before and after using the same criteria.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The token count and total volume by size mentioned in the document are assumptions for illustrative purposes. For actual conversion decisions, use the actual token count and cost per call.

checks.q: The search approach ensures that the input size per request remains relatively constant, even as the document volume grows. What is the reason behind this, and what are the trade-offs involved?

glossary.def: This method involves inserting the entire document into the prompt for processing in one go.
This approach involves splitting documents into chunks and indexing them, then retrieving only the relevant chunks for each request. It is also known as RAG.
This is the point at which the volume of documentation begins to outperform other structures in terms of cost, accuracy, and limits.
The frequency at which documents change. This affects index recreation and the cost of maintaining up-to-date information.

misconceptions.myth: A large window has appeared, so there's no need for a search method.
misconceptions.fact: If document traversal or input cost per call is burdensome, a search-based approach remains appropriate.

misconceptions.myth: The search method is always more accurate.
misconceptions.fact: If context is fragmented by token splitting, search may fail. Content missed by search is not visible to the model.

misconceptions.myth: Once a structure is defined, just keep using it.
misconceptions.fact: If the volume of documents or the frequency of updates changes, the transition point also changes, so the structure must be re-evaluated.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Scale and update frequency determine the structure.
Small and stable means a long context is simple and sufficient.
Larger or frequently changing data may be suitable for search, but it comes with operational overheads such as partitioning, embedding, and indexing.
Cost escalation, accuracy degradation, and window overflow are signals that the architecture needs to change.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: How much will my document volume increase over the next year, and will my current structure still be adequate at that time?
